title: the Nayanars
hook: two mangoes, one hungry guest, and a husband who wants the second one

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nayanars, the Tamil saints of Shiva, and Kannappa, the hunter who worshiped all wrong and gave his own eye. Whose clumsy kindness did you notice? Day nine hundred eleven.

Two mangoes arrive at a merchant's house in the port town of Karaikkal. The merchant has sent them home for his lunch. His wife, Punitavati, puts them aside. Then there's a knock: a wandering devotee of Shiva, worn out and hungry. She has rice ready but nothing to go with it, so she gives him rice and one of the mangoes. He eats, blesses her, and goes. Then her husband comes home, eats the remaining mango, loves it, and says: bring me the other one. Today's Nayanar is standing in her kitchen with nothing to bring.
screen: `TWO MANGOES.` → `ONE GOES TO A HUNGRY GUEST.` → `BRING ME THE OTHER ONE.`

segments.voice: The Periya Puranam tells it like this. Punitavati goes into the kitchen and prays to Shiva, and a mango appears in her hand. She serves it. It's sweeter than the first, so sweet that her husband asks where it came from. She tells him the truth. He doesn't quite believe her. Then get me another one, he says. She prays again, another mango appears, and the moment he takes it, it vanishes. Now he's afraid. Not angry: afraid. His wife is clearly something more than he bargained for. So he quietly sails away on business, settles in another town, marries again, and names his daughter Punitavati. When her family finally finds him, he bows down before her as if she were a goddess. Here's the turn. Punitavati doesn't ask for him back. The story says she asks Shiva to take away the beauty she kept for her husband and give her the form of a pey, a gaunt, skeletal ghost-like being. And it happens. Then she sets out for Shiva's mountain, and when she reaches it, the Periya Puranam says, she goes up it on her head, upside down, so her feet won't touch the holy ground. Shiva sees her coming and calls her Mother. From then on she's Karaikkal Ammaiyar, the mother of Karaikkal. She sings of Shiva dancing in the cremation ground, and asks only to stay at his feet, singing, while he dances. Notice what she gave away first: one mango, to a stranger, without asking anyone. Everything else in her story grows out of that small decision at the door.
screen: `A MANGO APPEARS IN HER HAND.` · `HE SAILS AWAY, AFRAID.` · `SHE ASKS TO LOSE HER BEAUTY.` · `SHIVA CALLS HER MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Picture your own front door, and someone knocking: a neighbor, a stranger, someone who needs something small. Notice what you'd have to give. Notice, too, the voice that says, save it, someone might ask for it later. You don't have to argue with that voice. Just breathe beside it for a while. If you pray, you can pray for whoever may knock on your door this week, in words you already know. The bell holds the time.
The Nayanars. The Tamil saints of Shiva. Karaikkal Ammaiyar is the woman of the mangoes, whom Shiva called Mother.
Your line: the Nayanars. Today, give one small thing at the door, without checking first whether you'll need it later. Day nine hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Karaikkal Ammaiyar is honored among the Nayanars in Shiva temples, and in Karaikkal a mango festival remembers the story of the two mangoes.

fork.setup: you're Punitavati. you gave one mango to a hungry guest, and now your husband asks for it. what do you do?
options: go into the kitchen and pray to Shiva.
send a servant to the market.
fork.reveal: she prays, and a mango appears in her hand, sweeter than the first. the miracle is what frightens her husband away.

original.note: Tamil: the mother of Karaikkal, the name given to Punitavati.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic mango trick.
what it means: a woman who gave to a stranger, lost a marriage, and asked for nothing back but Shiva.
what a scholar hears: she sings of Shiva dancing in the cremation ground, and the Periya Puranam tells her life among the Nayanars.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the Periya Puranam sequence: the two mangoes, the devotee, the miraculous mango, the vanishing one, the husband Paramadattan leaving by sea, remarrying and naming his daughter after her, bowing to her, her request for the pey form, walking up Kailasa (now 'on her head'), Shiva calling her 'Ammai'.
'Pey' glossed as 'a gaunt, skeletal ghost-like being'; confirm the gloss is respectful and accurate.

Audit: the climb up Kailasa was told as 'on her hands'; the Periya Puranam has her go on her head (talaiyal natantu). Teach and myth corrected to 'on her head'; some popular retellings say hands. Keeper to confirm.
Common claims that her poems are among the oldest in the Shaiva canon are deliberately left out under the claims rule.
